title: 1 Samuel 29:6–11
context: Achish praises David but sends him back at the commanders’ insistence. David protests, then leaves early in the morning while the Philistines go up to Jezreel, so he is kept from fighting against Israel.

verses.text: Then Achish called David and said to him, “As the LORD lives, you have been upright, and your going out and your coming in with me in the army is good in my sight; for I have not found evil in you since the day of your coming to me to this day. Nevertheless, the lords don’t favor you.
verses.arminianNotes: Achish says, “As the LORD lives, you have been upright,” but “the lords don’t favor you.” Arminian readers see a pagan king speaking warmly of David while still sending him away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Achish’s oath by the LORD as notable on a Philistine’s lips. The verdict of the lords prevails, and David is removed from the battle without having to choose sides.

verses.text: Therefore now return, and go in peace, that you not displease the lords of the Philistines.”
verses.arminianNotes: Achish says, “Therefore now return, and go in peace, that you not displease the lords of the Philistines.” Arminian readers see David released from the danger he had placed himself in.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a providential release from an impossible situation. The command to go in peace removes David from the battlefield where Saul will fall.

verses.text: David said to Achish, “But what have I done? What have you found in your servant so long as I have been before you to this day, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?”
verses.arminianNotes: David protests, “But what have I done? … that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?” Arminian readers see continued ambiguity in David’s words about whom he would fight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see David maintaining his cover. Interpreters differ on whether “my lord the king” is meant to suggest Achish or Saul, and the narrator leaves the phrase open.

verses.text: Achish answered David, “I know that you are good in my sight, as an angel of God. Notwithstanding, the princes of the Philistines have said, ‘He shall not go up with us to the battle.’
verses.arminianNotes: Achish says, “I know that you are good in my sight, as an angel of God,” yet the princes have said “He shall not go up with us.” Arminian readers see sincere praise outweighed by others’ decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Achish’s high regard and his limited authority. The decision of the princes stands, and David’s path is turned without any action of his own.

verses.text: Therefore now rise up early in the morning with the servants of your lord who have come with you; and as soon as you are up early in the morning and have light, depart.”
verses.arminianNotes: Achish tells David to rise early “and have light, depart.” Arminian readers see a firm instruction that sends David away before the armies engage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the timing of David’s departure. The next chapter shows he will need to return to Ziklag quickly, where trouble awaits him.

verses.text: So David rose up early, he and his men, to depart in the morning, to return into the land of the Philistines; and the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
verses.arminianNotes: David and his men leave in the morning, while the Philistines go up to Jezreel. Arminian readers see the paths of David and Saul diverging just before Saul’s final battle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see providence separating David from the battle that ends Saul’s reign. Readers in both traditions commonly see God’s hand in David being kept from fighting his own people.
